title: Rosetta/Mars Express Mission Control System (RMCS/MEMCS) Data Delivery Interface Document DDID
organisation: European Space Agency, ESOC (Rosetta / MEX Ground Segment Teams)
status_notes: Issue B5, 2003/03/27 (PDF p. 1), updated according to the DDID review of 18 December 2002. The approval pages (PDF pp. 3-4) list ESOC, ESTEC and contractor (Anite) approvers and the Rosetta and Mars Express PIs, with blank signature lines. Superseded by later issues (B6 to C2; see library item ro-esc-if-5003-ddid-c2), which also added Venus Express.
summary:
Issue B5 (27 March 2003) of the Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID) shared by the Rosetta and Mars Express mission control systems (RMCS/MEMCS) at ESOC, RO-ESC-IF-5003 / MEX-ESC-IF-5003. This copy was distributed inside the Mars Express Radio Science (MRS) archive in ESA's Planetary Science Archive. The DDID is the ICD between the SCOS-2000-based mission control systems and the science communities; with the Command Request Interface Document it defines the complete PI interface. The text says this is the twelfth update and the sixth issue, re-integrating Mars Express with Rosetta.

The structure and most content match the later issue C2. It covers the Data Disposition System (DDS) requirements (FTP or web requests, 15-minute response, quotas, sampling every Nth packet, automatic forwarding), interface characteristics, access and security, and generation from the MCS Data Archive System. The data definition chapter specifies the XML on-line request, responses, acknowledgements and catalogue entries in SFDU packaging; telemetry delivered as reconstituted source packets with an 18-octet DDS packet header (SCET, length, ground station ID, VC, SLE type, time quality); command history with a DDS command header carrying CUV, CAV and CEV verification flags; auxiliary data, catalogues, error messages and RDM (CD-ROM) layouts. Appendices cover data streams and ADIDs, error handling, the MEX RDM listing, auxiliary data types, an SFDU tutorial, nomenclature conventions, MCS products (APID 1966/type 190 internal packets, time correlation, lander TC verification file, detailed agenda file) and the science network implementation.

Compared with issue C2, this issue still speaks of on-line 'quick-look' data, gives a 3-week (TBC) RDM delivery target, splits RDM days by SCOS-2000 packet generation time, has fewer ground station IDs (NASA Madrid TBD), and leaves Appendices C (accounts) and I (XML schema) to separate documents. It is useful for tracing how the ESOC data delivery interface evolved.

key_points.text: The DDID defines the data delivery interface between the Rosetta and Mars Express mission control systems (RMCS and MEMCS) at ESOC and their science communities, through the Data Disposition System (DDS); in this issue the on-line data are called 'quick-look' data.
Section 1.4 states this is the twelfth update of the DDID and the sixth issue, and section 1.5 that it re-integrates Mars Express with the Rosetta interface requirements and design.
RDMs are to be delivered within 3 weeks (TBC) of reception at the OCC, and the split by day uses the SCOS-2000 packet generation time (equivalent to the archive time).

Each delivered telemetry packet carries an 18-octet DDS packet header: SCET (two 32-bit integers, seconds and microseconds since 1970), packet length, ground station ID (e.g. 0x15 Kourou, 0x17 New Norcia, 0x22 Goldstone, 0x23 Canberra, NASA Madrid TBD), virtual channel, SLE service type and time quality.
For on-line data the DDS shall provide access for 3 months (TBC) after acquisition from the spacecraft.
Appendix C (accounts) and Appendix I (request dialogue XML schema) are provided as separate documents (A-8 and A-7).
MCS-internal telemetry packets that carry no identification of their own are identified by APID 1966 and type 190.

notes: The file name says 'B5' and the content agrees (Issue B5, 2003/03/27); it was retrieved from the ESA PSA Mars Express Radio Science archive (MEX-ESC-IF-5003.PDF). Body page offset: printed page 1 is PDF p. 23 (PDF page = printed page + 22). The table of contents is out of step with the body for the appendices (for example it gives Appendix D at page 100 while the body prints it on page 86, because Appendices C and I are only placeholders here). The text layer shows ordinal suffixes ('th', 'st') on separate lines and change-tracking markers such as 'DCR218' and '039' inserted into the text. Appendix C refers to an applicable document A-8 that is not in the A-1 to A-7 list. Appendix J is marked TBW. Content largely duplicates the later issue C2 (library item ro-esc-if-5003-ddid-c2); key points here focus on differences.
